given:
Research current, citable evidence to ground a plan for someone whose goal is sustainable fat loss. Focus on what actually moves this goal: a realistic rate of change, protein and calorie targets, and anything specific to their situation below.

Their own words about their goal + life:
"Timeframe: by june, no rush really
Day-to-day: desk job 9 to 5:30. i usually skip breakfast and just have an iced latte, lunch is whatever's near the office, i cook dinner most nights. i snack a lot around 4pm when i'm tired
Exercise & schedule: walk the dog every morning, like 30 min. pilates tuesday and thursday evenings. hike on weekends when the weather's ok"

Return the cited findings now (no plan yet).
output:
## Evidence brief for sustainable fat loss

**Time horizon and rate**

- Assuming “by June” means **June 2027**, there are roughly **27–31 weeks** from November 25, 2026. A gradual pace is appropriate given “no rush.”
- The CDC describes **1–2 lb/week (0.45–0.9 kg/week)** as a generally reasonable upper range, but slower loss is still meaningful and may be easier to sustain. A useful initial health target is approximately **5% of starting body weight**, rather than an arbitrary scale number. ([cdc.gov](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-weight-growth/losing-weight/?CDC_AAref_Val=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.cdc.gov%2Fhealthyweight%2Flosing_weight%2F&utm_source=openai))
- For preserving lean mass, especially as someone becomes leaner, current sports-nutrition evidence favors avoiding aggressive deficits; around **0.5–0.7% of body weight per week or less** is a conservative ceiling. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/15502783.2026.2743880?utm_source=openai))

**Calories**

- Fat loss requires a sustained energy deficit; no particular diet composition—low-fat, low-carbohydrate, fasting, etc.—is consistently superior when calorie intake and adherence are comparable. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1530891X25009772?utm_source=openai))
- Current clinical guidance commonly starts with approximately a **500–750 kcal/day deficit**, or roughly **10–30% below maintenance**, then adjusts from observed weight trends. The smaller end is more consistent with this person’s relaxed timeline. ([healthquality.va.gov](https://healthquality.va.gov/HEALTHQUALITY/guidelines/CD/obesity/OBE-CPG_2025-Guideline_final_20251105.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- An actual calorie target **cannot be responsibly calculated** without age, sex, height and current weight. When measured energy expenditure is unavailable, the 2025 VA/DoD guideline identifies the **Mifflin–St Jeor equation using actual body weight** as a reasonable estimate; the NIDDK Body Weight Planner can model how calorie needs change over time. ([healthquality.va.gov](https://healthquality.va.gov/HEALTHQUALITY/guidelines/CD/obesity/OBE-CPG_2025-Guideline_final_20251105.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**Protein and muscle retention**

- For a generally healthy adult losing fat, a practical evidence-based protein range is **1.2–1.6 g/kg of body weight per day**. Exercising adults may reasonably use **1.4–2.0 g/kg/day**, with the upper end becoming more relevant during resistance training or larger deficits. ([tandfonline.com](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/15502783.2026.2740266?needAccess=true&utm_source=openai))
- Protein and progressive resistance training work together to reduce lean-mass loss during calorie restriction. Recent meta-analysis also finds that resistance exercise during diet-induced weight loss protects fat-free mass and improves strength. ([doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1080/15502783.2026.2740266?utm_source=openai))
- Higher protein targets may need medical modification with **chronic kidney disease or certain other conditions**. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13671912/?utm_source=openai))

**Specific implications of the stated routine**

- **Skipping breakfast is not inherently a problem.** Randomized-trial evidence does not show that eating breakfast itself causes better weight loss. The relevant issue is whether the current pattern—including the iced latte, office lunch and 4 p.m. snacks—keeps total calories and protein aligned with the target. ([bmj.com](https://www.bmj.com/content/364/bmj.l42?utm_source=openai))
- The **iced latte counts toward energy intake**; depending on size, milk and sweeteners, beverages can materially affect the deficit even when they are not perceived as a meal.
- The described dog walking provides about **210 minutes/week of walking**, but whether it meets moderate-intensity guidance depends on pace. Pilates twice weekly may provide some muscular stimulus, though
